Source: Smoke: JAX

title: Run it yourself
text: Every page on this site is built from notebooks you can run on your own CUDA GPU.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Requirements

Linux with an NVIDIA GPU and a recent driver (tested: driver 580, CUDA 13.0)
juliaup (the project pins Julia 1.12)
uv for the Python/JAX environment
Quarto ≥ 1.10
make

title: Run it yourself
text:
Install
git clone https://github.com/michel2323/WEANJ
cd WEANJ
make setup
make setup installs the Julia 1.12 channel, instantiates and precompiles the Julia environment in julia/ (Enzyme, Reactant, CUDA), creates the Python environment in python/ (JAX with CUDA 13), and writes _environment.local so Quarto uses that Python. The first run downloads several GB and takes 10–15 minutes.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Check the toolchain
quarto render smoke/
This runs a tiny gradient on the GPU with each of the three tools. Open _site/smoke/index.html; all three tabs should show output.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Run the examples
quarto preview                      # browse the site, edit and re-run notebooks live
quarto render examples/01-particles/enzyme.qmd   # re-run one notebook
make run-gpu                        # re-run everything; refreshes _freeze/ and benchmarks/
Rendering a single notebook always executes it. Rendering the whole site uses the frozen outputs in _freeze/, so it does not need a GPU.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Troubleshooting

JAX prints CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY

Another process is using the GPU. The notebooks disable JAX’s up-front memory reservation, but benchmark numbers are only meaningful on an idle GPU: make gpu-check lists what is running.

Julia version mismatch

The notebooks start Julia with julia +1.12. Run juliaup add 1.12.

title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Note



Work in progress. The examples are being added one at a time; see the project plan.
“Why do you use Julia instead of JAX?” is a fair question, and “JAX can’t sort” is the wrong answer: jax.lax.sort is differentiable. The real difference is the execution model.
JAX differentiates pure functions over fixed-shape arrays with a static computation graph. Anything that fits that model runs well, often better than hand-written code, because XLA fuses and vectorises it. Enzyme differentiates the imperative program as written, including in-place mutation, data-dependent loop bounds and growing buffers. When an algorithm’s efficient form is irregular, JAX makes you regularise it with padding, masks, static trip counts or implicit differentiation. Enzyme lets you keep it.
Each example below implements the same loss three times, with Enzyme.jl, with Reactant.jl, and with JAX, checks that all three give the same gradient, and times them on a CUDA GPU. Reactant is the control: it is Julia compiled through XLA, the same static-graph model as JAX. Where Reactant hits the same wall as JAX, the cause is the execution model, not the language.

title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Where the gap shows up

Data-dependent output size or sparsity

Compaction and filtering (x[mask], push!), sparse assembly with data-dependent fill-in, contact detection, tree codes (octrees, Barnes–Hut). JAX needs a static upper bound and masks.

Data-dependent control flow

Iterative solvers with convergence tests, adaptive time stepping. JAX cannot reverse-differentiate lax.while_loop, so you fix the iteration count or switch to implicit differentiation.

Sequential in-place updates

Gauss–Seidel, SOR, Thomas algorithm, sweeps where element i depends on the just-updated i−1. In JAX these become lax.scan with the whole array as carry, and reverse mode stores every carry unless you rematerialise.

Irregular neighbour access

Particle methods with cell lists (sort by cell, loop over a data-dependent number of neighbours), scatter-accumulate with data-dependent indices, histogramming, resampling.

title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Where JAX wins
Dense, batched, regular work: most of machine learning, many PDE stencils, anything whose naive cost already equals its smart cost. There the regularised JAX version is often faster despite padding, because XLA fuses and the hardware wants regular access. And the advantage on this site is Enzyme’s, not Julia’s: Julia AD tools that do not support mutation (Zygote) cannot do this either.

title: Methodology
text: How the comparisons are made, so they can be checked and reproduced.

title: Methodology
text:
Same inputs
Inputs for each example are generated once in Julia with a fixed seed and written to data/<example>.npz. All three implementations load that file.

title: Methodology
text:
Same gradient
Every implementation computes the gradient of the same loss at the same point in Float64 and saves it to benchmarks/grads/<example>_<impl>.npz. Each example page checks that

every gradient agrees with central finite differences on a few random components, and
all three gradients agree with each other (relative tolerance 1e-8).

A failing check fails the build, so a published page always shows matching gradients.

title: Methodology
text:
Timing

Timing runs use Float32, as is usual on GPUs; the correctness check uses Float64.
Compile time (first call) is reported separately from run time. It matters for JAX and Reactant, which compile a whole graph, and for Enzyme, which compiles on first call.
Run time is the median of 10 calls after 2 warm-up calls. GPU work is synchronised inside the timed region (CUDA.synchronize, jax.block_until_ready).
Problem size N is swept over several orders of magnitude so scaling is visible, not just one data point.
Peak device memory is reported where the tool exposes it.
Benchmarks run on an otherwise idle GPU (make gpu-check refuses to run otherwise).

title: Methodology
section: Fairness rules for the JAX column
text:
Fairness rules for the JAX column
The JAX code is what a competent JAX user would write, not a literal translation:

jax.jit everything, donate buffers where it helps, and use jax.checkpoint where a practitioner would.
Use the ecosystem’s own tools where they exist: jax-md cell and neighbour lists, Optimistix for implicit differentiation, Diffrax for adaptive time stepping.
Where JAX needs a static capacity (padding), size it from the data and handle overflow the way jax-md does, and report the padding overhead.
Every example page has a “Where JAX wins / what we did not do” note.

title: Methodology
text:
Hardware and software
Results on the published site were produced on an NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada Generation Laptop GPU (16 GB), Julia 1.12, Enzyme.jl 0.13, Reactant.jl 0.2, JAX 0.11 (CUDA 13). Exact versions are pinned in julia/Manifest.toml and python/uv.lock.
